flags.heading: The flags
flags.none: Not enough data came back to raise any flags.
basis.units: For this building, the rates use {count} from PLUTO.

rules.1: Open Class C (immediately hazardous) HPD violations: 3 or more is a red flag when that is also at least 1 for every {every} apartments; any other number above zero is yellow; none is green.
rules.2: Open Class B (hazardous) HPD violations: 10 or more, and at least 1 for every {every} apartments, is a yellow flag.
rules.3: Open HPD violations mentioning lead paint: any is a red flag.
rules.4: Open HPD violations mentioning pests or mold: any is a yellow flag.
rules.5: Heat or hot water 311 complaints in the last 2 years: 10 or more, and at least 1 for every {red} apartments, is red; 3 or more, and at least 1 for every {yellow} apartments, is yellow; none is green.
rules.6: Plumbing or leak 311 complaints in the last 2 years: 10 or more, and at least 1 for every {every} apartments, is a yellow flag.
rules.7: Elevator 311 complaints in the last 2 years: 5 or more is a yellow flag. This stays a plain count, since one elevator serves the whole building.
rules.8: Active DOB complaints about safety or upkeep: any is a yellow flag. No DOB complaints in 3 years is green.
rules.9: Residential evictions in the last 5 years: 6 or more, and at least 1 for every {red} apartments, is red; 2 or more, and at least 1 for every {yellow} apartments, is yellow; none is green.
rules.10: Apartment counts: the “for every N apartments” parts use the residential unit count for the whole tax lot from the city’s PLUTO data, the same lot the violation, 311 and eviction counts cover. A small building clears the rate as soon as it clears the count, so its flags work just as before. When PLUTO has no apartment count for the lot (or doesn’t load), those parts are skipped and the plain counts alone decide.
rules.11: Currently in HPD’s Alternative Enforcement Program (the city’s list of buildings with the worst conditions): red flag. If the listing is for a different building on the same tax lot, yellow. A past, finished AEP listing is shown but not flagged.
rules.12: HPD vacate order that hasn’t been lifted (no rescind date on or before today): red flag, or yellow if it’s for a different building on the same tax lot. Lifted orders are shown but not flagged.
rules.13: HPD housing court cases opened in the last 5 years: 15 or more is red, 5 to 14 is yellow, none is green. Any case still pending makes it at least yellow. If none of the lot’s cases match this exact building, the lot’s cases are counted and labeled that way.
rules.14: An HPD court finding of tenant harassment in the last 5 years: red flag.
rules.15: Landlord’s latest bedbug filing, only if its reporting year ended in the last 2 years: 5 or more infested apartments, or 10% or more of the apartments, is red; any other number above zero is yellow. Zero infested, or no filing at all, raises no flag either way. If we can’t match this exact building on a tax lot with several buildings, the newest filing of each building on the lot is added up.
rules.16: Mascot mood: 2 or more red or 4 or more yellow flags means worried; 1 red or 2 or 3 yellow means mixed; otherwise happy.
rules.context1: How it compares, the trend and the fix rate are context only. They never add or remove a flag and never change the mascot’s mood.
rules.context2: How it compares: open HPD violations (Class A, B and C) divided by the lot’s apartment count, placed among every tax lot in the same borough and size group (1 or 2 apartments, or 3 or more) in a snapshot of NYC Open Data. Lots with no open violations count as zero. The snapshot stores each group’s percentiles, so the share is given to the nearest point and always says “about”.
rules.context3: Trend: HPD violations issued plus 311 complaints about conditions in the building, in the last 12 full months compared with the 12 months before. At least {upPct} more (and at least {minChange} more) reads as climbing; at least {downPct} fewer (and at least {minChange} fewer) reads as eased; anything else reads as about steady. Fewer than {minReports} reports across both years is too few to call.
rules.context4: Fix rate: of the HPD violations issued in the last 5 years, the share whose status is closed (HPD counts dismissed ones as closed too). The typical fix is the median number of days from the notice to the date the status changed to closed, shown once at least {minClosed} are closed. “More than a year old” counts open Class A, B and C violations issued over a year ago.

q.heading: Questions to ask the landlord
q.intro: Built from the flags above. Ask them out loud and see what you learn.
q.class-c: HPD lists open Class C (immediately hazardous) violations here. Which ones affect this unit, and when will they be fixed?
q.class-b: There are a number of open Class B violations on record. What is the plan and timeline for clearing them?
q.lead: Some open violations mention lead paint. Has this apartment been tested or treated for lead, and can I see the results?
q.pests: The record shows violations about pests. How often is the building treated, and has this unit had any issues?
q.mold: Mold shows up in the open violations. Has this unit had mold or leaks, and how was it addressed?
q.heat: Tenants have called 311 about heat or hot water. How old is the boiler, and how are outages handled in winter?
q.plumbing: There are recurring plumbing or leak complaints. Have there been any leaks in or above this unit?
q.elevator: Elevator complaints come up in 311. How often is it out of service, and how quickly is it repaired?
q.dob-active: The Department of Buildings has active complaints on file. What are they about, and are they resolved?
q.evictions: The public record shows evictions at this address. How are rent disputes or late payments usually handled?
q.aep: The building is in HPD’s Alternative Enforcement Program. What repairs are planned, and what is the timeline for finishing them?
q.vacate: HPD has a vacate order on record here that hasn’t been lifted. What is it for, and does it affect this apartment?
q.litigation: There are HPD housing court cases on record. What were they about, and have the issues been fixed?
q.harassment: An HPD court case here found tenant harassment. What has changed in how the building is managed since then?
q.bedbugs: The latest bedbug filing reports infested apartments. Has this unit or its neighbors been treated, and when?
q.longOpen_one: HPD lists 1 violation from {year} that is still open after more than a year. What is the plan to close it?
q.longOpen_other: HPD lists {n} violations that are still open after more than a year, the oldest from {year}. What is the plan to close them?
q.trendUp: Reports to HPD and 311 have gone up over the last year. What is behind the increase, and what is being done about it?
q.vacateHistory: HPD issued a vacate order here ({reason}) that was later lifted. What happened, and what was repaired?
q.vacateHistoryYear: HPD issued a vacate order here in {year} ({reason}) that was later lifted. What happened, and what was repaired?
q.recentSale: A new deed for this building was recorded in {year}. Is there new ownership or management, and are any renovations or rent changes planned?
q.general1: Who do I contact for repairs, and what is the typical response time?
q.general2: Is this apartment rent stabilized? Can I see the rent history?

fare.entry.title: Charged a broker fee?
fare.entry.body: New York City changed the rules in June 2025. Answer a few questions and see whether the fee you paid, or are being asked to pay, matches what the law allows.
fare.results.title: About to sign? Check the fee first
fare.results.body: If anyone asks you for a broker fee on this home, run the two minute check before you pay it.
fare.listingHint: This listing mentions a fee. There is a quick check for whether a charge like that is one you should be paying at all.
fare.heading: Check a broker fee
fare.intro: Since June 11, 2025, a New York City law called the FARE Act says the person who hires the broker pays the broker. If the broker works for the landlord, that cost is the landlord’s, not yours. This check lines your answers up against the law and shows you what people in your spot usually do next.
fare.privacy: Your answers stay on this device. Nothing is sent or stored.
fare.q.signed: When were you charged the fee, or when are you being asked to pay it?
fare.q.signed.help: The date that matters is the charge, not the day you signed the lease. A fee charged on or after June 11, 2025 falls under the FARE Act even on a lease signed earlier, if the fee had not been paid yet.
fare.a.signed.notYet: I have not paid yet. They are asking now
fare.q.hired.help: If the broker was advertising the apartment, showing it, or works with the landlord, the law treats them as the landlord’s broker. A broker counts as yours only if you went out and hired one yourself to search for you.
fare.a.hired.me: I hired my own broker to search for me
fare.a.hired.landlord: The broker was showing or advertising this apartment
fare.q.extra: Were you charged anything beyond the basics?
fare.q.extra.help: The basics are the first month of rent, a deposit of one month of rent or less, and an application fee of $20 or less. Anything else counts here, whatever it was called.
fare.charges.intro: List each extra charge, using the words they used.
fare.charges.label: What was it called?
fare.q.paper: Did anyone have you sign a paper about the broker?
fare.q.paper.help: Some renters are handed a form saying they hired the broker, sometimes in a stack of papers at signing. Reports since the law describe this as a common workaround, so it is worth remembering whether you saw one.
fare.a.paper.yes: Yes, I signed something like that
fare.q.rent.help: Optional. It only helps show what the charges add up to next to a year of rent, and whether a deposit was bigger than one month.
fare.level.green: Your answers look consistent with the law
fare.level.red: Your answers match the pattern the law bans
fare.blurb.green: Nothing in your answers stands out as a charge the law takes issue with. Keep your paperwork anyway; it is your proof if anything changes.
fare.blurb.yellow: A few answers could go either way, and the missing detail is usually the one that decides it. Below is what would settle each point, and what you can do either way.
fare.blurb.red: One or more charges line up with what the FARE Act and related rules say a renter should not be paying. Below is the rule for each charge, and the steps people take to get the money back.
fare.rule.heading: The rule, and your answers
fare.rule.yes: The FARE Act reaches your situation: the charge was made on or after June 11, 2025, when the law took effect.
fare.rule.no: The charge was made before June 11, 2025, so the FARE Act itself does not reach it. Older New York rules still capped application fees at $20 and deposits at one month of rent, and those caps are part of this check.
fare.rule.unsure: The date of the charge decides whether the FARE Act reaches it: the law covers charges made on or after June 11, 2025. If you can pin down the date, your picture gets much clearer.
fare.rule.hired.me: You hired your own broker. Paying a broker you chose yourself is still allowed, and it is the main exception to the rule.
fare.rule.hired.landlord: The broker was the landlord’s side: advertising or showing the apartment. Under the FARE Act, a broker working for the landlord is paid by the landlord.
fare.rule.hired.unsure: Who hired the broker is the heart of the law. A broker who listed or showed the home is treated as the landlord’s broker, even if they were friendly and helpful to you.
fare.rule.caps: Two older caps also apply everywhere in New York: an application fee can be at most $20, and a security deposit can be at most one month of rent. A landlord also cannot ask for rent in advance beyond the first month.
fare.reason.landlordBrokerFee: A broker charge from the landlord’s side is the exact pattern the FARE Act bans.
fare.reason.applicationOver: An application fee above $20 breaks the state cap, whatever it was called.
fare.reason.depositOver: A deposit or advance above one month of rent breaks the state cap of one month.
fare.reason.paperSigned: You signed a paper saying you hired the broker. When the broker was really the landlord’s, reports describe this paper as a workaround, and it is worth raising in any complaint.
fare.reason.paperUnsure: You may have signed a paper about hiring the broker. If one exists, what it says matters, so it is worth asking for your copy.
fare.reason.dateUnsure: The date of the charge is unconfirmed, and it decides whether the FARE Act applies.
fare.reason.hiredUnsure: It is unconfirmed whose broker this was, and that is the fact the law turns on.
fare.reason.someUnclear: At least one charge does not fit neatly into a rule, so it sits in the unclear column.
fare.reason.beforeLaw: The broker charge predates the FARE Act, so the ban does not reach it.
fare.reason.noExtras: You reported no charges beyond the basics.
fare.reason.allConsistent: Every charge you listed fits within what the law allows.
fare.charges.heading: Your charges, lined up
fare.yearShare: That is {share} of a full year of rent.
fare.charges.none: No extra charges to line up.
fare.charge.brokerOwn: You hired this broker yourself, so paying them is allowed. This is the exception the law keeps.
fare.charge.brokerBefore: This charge was made before the FARE Act took effect, so the ban does not reach it.
fare.charge.brokerLandlord: The broker was working for the landlord, and the charge came after the law took effect. The FARE Act says the landlord pays their own broker.
fare.charge.brokerDate: If this charge was made on or after June 11, 2025, the FARE Act says the landlord pays their own broker. The date is what decides it.
fare.charge.brokerUnsure: Everything turns on whose broker this was. If they listed or showed the apartment, the law counts them as the landlord’s broker.
fare.charge.otherFeeLandlord: A fee under another name, charged on the landlord’s side after the law took effect, matches the pattern the FARE Act bans. Changing the label does not change the rule.
fare.charge.otherFeeUnsure: Fees under other names are how this charge often hides. Whose side the broker was on, and the date, decide where this lands.
fare.charge.applicationNoAmount: Application fees are capped at ${cap}. Without the amount, this one cannot be lined up against the cap.
fare.charge.applicationOver: Application fees are capped at ${cap} in New York. Anything above that matches a pattern the law bans, whatever the charge was called.
fare.charge.applicationUnder: At or under the ${cap} cap for application fees, so this one fits the rule.
fare.charge.depositNoRent: A deposit can be at most one month of rent. Add the monthly rent to line this one up.
fare.charge.depositOver: This is more than one month of rent. New York caps a security deposit at one month, so the part above one month matches a banned pattern.
fare.charge.depositUnder: One month of rent or less, so this deposit fits the cap.
fare.charge.advanceNoRent: Rent in advance is limited to the first month. Add the monthly rent to line this one up.
fare.charge.advanceOver: This is more than the first month of rent. Asking for rent in advance beyond the first month matches a pattern state law bans.
fare.charge.advanceUnder: No more than the first month, so this fits the rule.
fare.charge.other: This charge does not match a label the rules speak to directly. The written ask below still covers it: whoever charged it can be asked to name the rule that allows it.
fare.next.heading: What to do next
fare.next.intro: Three steps, in order. The first one solves many cases on its own.
fare.next.script: Ask for the money back, in writing
fare.next.scriptNote: A template, in your words. Fill in the blanks, keep a copy, and send it somewhere you can prove it went, like email.
fare.evidence.lease: Your lease, and anything you signed at the same table
fare.evidence.receipts: Receipts, bank lines, or card statements showing each charge
fare.evidence.listing: The listing itself: screenshots and the web address, showing any fee it mentioned
fare.evidence.messages: Messages and emails with the broker or landlord about the fee
fare.evidence.paper: Any paper saying you hired the broker, if you signed one
fare.evidence.notes: Your own notes: dates, names, and who said what
fare.next.routes: File a complaint, or go to court
fare.route.dcwp: File with DCWP, the city consumer agency
fare.route.dcwp.note: The Department of Consumer and Worker Protection enforces the FARE Act. File online or call 311 and say broker fees. They mediate and can order money back, and you can file even about a listing you only saw.
fare.route.dos: Report the broker to the state
fare.route.dos.note: Brokers are licensed by the New York Department of State. A complaint there goes on the broker’s license record.
fare.route.court.note: The FARE Act also gives you the right to sue for the money yourself. Small claims court in New York City handles claims up to $10,000 and is built for people without a lawyer.
fare.script.paidLine: I am writing about the charges I paid for the apartment: {charges}. The total was {total}.
fare.script.law.broker: Under the FARE Act, in effect since June 11, 2025, a broker who represents the landlord is paid by the landlord, not by the tenant.
fare.script.law.application: Under New York law, an application fee is capped at $20.
fare.script.law.deposit: Under New York law, a security deposit is capped at one month of rent, and rent cannot be collected in advance beyond the first month.
fare.script.askBack: Please return {total} to me. If you believe a charge was allowed, please point me to the rule that allows it.
fare.script.askBasis: I am writing about the charges listed here: {charges}. Please explain, in writing, what each charge is for and the rule that allows it.
fare.script.records: I have kept my lease, my receipts, and our messages, and I am happy to share copies.
fare.script.signoff: Thank you for looking at this. I would like to settle it directly with you.
fare.disclaimer: This is public information about the law, not legal advice. For advice about your lease, a tenant lawyer or a legal aid clinic can help.
fare.sources: Rules summarized from the FARE Act (Local Law 119 of 2024) and New York State housing law, as published by NYC DCWP and the NYC Council.
